title: Smallest Range Covering Elements from K Lists
description: Find the smallest range including at least one element from each of k sorted lists, using a min-heap k-way merge with a running maximum.

content.title: Smallest Range Covering Elements from K Lists

blocks.text: Given k lists of sorted integers, find the smallest range [start, end] that includes at least one number from each of the k lists. If multiple ranges are equally small, return the one with the smallest start.

blocks.caption: A min-heap tracks the current smallest pointer value across all lists, while a running maximum tracks the largest.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","k lists, each individually sorted ascending"],["Output","[start, end], the smallest range containing at least one element from every list"],["Tie-break","Among equally small ranges, prefer the smaller start"]]}

blocks.text: Needing "the current smallest among k pointers, one per sorted list" is the classic k-way merge pattern, solved with a min-heap holding one candidate per list. Advancing only the SMALLEST pointer at each step (since it is the one holding back the range from shrinking) while tracking a running maximum finds every relevant candidate range in order.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: This is the same k-way-merge min-heap technique used for problems like merging k sorted lists, adapted here to track a RANGE (min to max across all pointers) rather than merging into one combined sequence.

Picture one runner starting at the front of each sorted list, all moving forward together. At any moment, the range from the slowest (smallest value) runner to the fastest (largest value) runner is a valid candidate, since it spans at least one value from every list. Advancing the SLOWEST runner is always the best move, since only advancing them can possibly shrink this range further.

blocks.caption: Advancing the slowest runner is the only move that can shrink the current range.

items: Seed a min-heap with the first element of every list, and track the running maximum across all current pointers.
Repeatedly pop the minimum (the current worst/slowest pointer); measure the range against the running maximum, updating the best answer if smaller.
Advance ONLY the list the minimum came from; if that list runs out, no further range can include all k lists, so stop.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: The smallest range found across the full sweep is [20, 24] (width 4), matching the expected output exactly. This range includes 24 from list0, 20 from list1, and 22 from list2.

A direct approach re-scans all k current pointer values on every step to find both the minimum and maximum, advancing the list holding the minimum. This is correct but costs O(k) per step instead of O(log k).

A min-heap answers "which list currently holds the minimum" in O(log k), while a separately tracked running maximum (updated only when a new, larger value is pushed) avoids ever rescanning all k pointers just to find the maximum.
At each step, scan all k current pointer values directly to find both the minimum (to advance) and maximum (to measure the range).

codes.python:
def smallest_range(nums):
    k = len(nums)
    pointers = [0] * k
    best_start, best_end = -float('inf'), float('inf')

    while True:
        cur_min = min(nums[i][pointers[i]] for i in range(k))
        cur_max = max(nums[i][pointers[i]] for i in range(k))

        if cur_max - cur_min < best_end - best_start:
            best_start, best_end = cur_min, cur_max

        min_list = min(range(k), key=lambda i: nums[i][pointers[i]])
        pointers[min_list] += 1
        if pointers[min_list] == len(nums[min_list]):
            break

    return [best_start, best_end]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(smallest_range([[4, 10, 15, 24, 26], [0, 9, 12, 20], [5, 18, 22, 30]]))
    print(smallest_range([[1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3]]))

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: Rescanning all k pointers every step to find the minimum is unnecessary once a min-heap can answer that in O(log k).

Seed a min-heap with the first element (value, list index, position) from every list, and track a running maximum. Repeatedly pop the minimum, compare the range (runningMax - poppedValue) against the best found, then advance that list's pointer, pushing its next value and updating the running maximum. Stop the moment any list is exhausted, since no range can then cover all k lists.

items: Seed the heap with one entry per list, O(k log k), tracking the initial running maximum.
Each step: pop the min (O(log k)), measure the range, push the next element of that list if one exists (O(log k)), update the running maximum.
Stop when any list is exhausted.

codes.python:
import heapq


def smallest_range(nums):
    k = len(nums)
    heap = []
    cur_max = -float('inf')

    for i in range(k):
        heapq.heappush(heap, (nums[i][0], i, 0))
        cur_max = max(cur_max, nums[i][0])

    best_start, best_end = -float('inf'), float('inf')

    while True:
        val, list_idx, elem_idx = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if cur_max - val < best_end - best_start:
            best_start, best_end = val, cur_max

        elem_idx += 1
        if elem_idx == len(nums[list_idx]):
            break

        next_val = nums[list_idx][elem_idx]
        cur_max = max(cur_max, next_val)
        heapq.heappush(heap, (next_val, list_idx, elem_idx))

    return [best_start, best_end]


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(smallest_range([[4, 10, 15, 24, 26], [0, 9, 12, 20], [5, 18, 22, 30]]))
    print(smallest_range([[1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3], [1, 2, 3]]))

items: A min-heap of one candidate per sorted list is the standard k-way-merge technique for "which list currently holds the smallest/next value."
Advancing only the list holding the current minimum is always the correct greedy move for shrinking a min-to-max range across multiple pointers.
Tracking the running maximum separately (updated only on push) avoids ever needing to rescan all k pointers just to find it.

blocks.text: Smallest Range Covering Elements from K Lists is solved with a min-heap holding one pointer per list, paired with a running maximum. Repeatedly advancing the list holding the current minimum, while tracking the smallest range seen, finds the answer in O(n log k) time, the classic k-way-merge pattern adapted to range-tracking instead of full merging.
